sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading

opts.A: It compiles, and save(5) calls whichever definition appears first in the class; the second definition is silently ignored
opts.B: It compiles and forms a valid overload pair, with the const version selected only when save is called through a const object
opts.C: It fails to compile: a top-level const on a pass-by-value parameter is not part of the function's parameter-type list, so both lines declare the exact same function, and giving that one function two separate bodies is a redefinition error
opts.D: It compiles, but calling save(5) is ambiguous and must be disambiguated with an explicit cast

exp: A const on a by-value parameter only stops the function body from reassigning its own local copy; it is invisible to callers and plays no part in the function's type, so int x and const int x describe one function, not two, and defining it twice is a redefinition error. B is the tempting mistake — const genuinely does distinguish overloads for a reference or pointer parameter (const T& versus T&), but never for a plain by-value one.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A Meters class has a non-explicit converting constructor from int and needs to support both m + 5 and 5 + m. operator+ is currently a member function, Meters operator+(const Meters& other) const. Why does this signature fail for 5 + m, and what is the fix?

opts.A: Nothing needs to change: the compiler automatically retries the reversed order on a member operator+ whenever the forward order fails to compile
opts.B: A member operator function's left operand is always the object it is called through, so 5 + m would require int to have a member operator+; making operator+ a free function, Meters operator+(const Meters&, const Meters&), lets the converting constructor apply to either argument and satisfies both orders
opts.C: The member function must instead be declared static, so that it no longer has an implicit first argument
opts.D: The fix is to add a second member overload, Meters operator+(int) const, inside the same class; that alone makes 5 + m compile

exp: m.operator+(5) works for m + 5 because a member operator's left operand is fixed to the object it is invoked on, but there is no way to write 5.operator+(m) since int has no members — so 5 + m can only compile if operator+ is a free function, letting overload resolution apply Meters's converting constructor to whichever argument needs it. D fails because an added member operator+(int) still only fixes the m + 5 order; it does nothing for 5 + m, where m is not the left operand.

sub: Polymorphism, function and operator overloading
q: A Vector class defines Vector& operator+=(const Vector& rhs); as a member function and wants to implement operator+ in terms of it, without duplicating the addition logic. Which is the canonical way to define operator+ so that a + b leaves both a and b unchanged?

opts.A: Vector& operator+(const Vector& rhs) { *this += rhs; return *this; } written as a member function, so that a + b mutates a and returns a reference to it
opts.B: Vector& operator+(const Vector& lhs, const Vector& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }, mutating and returning the caller's own lhs object directly
opts.C: Vector operator+(const Vector& lhs, const Vector& rhs) { return lhs += rhs; }, calling operator+= directly through the const reference
opts.D: Vector operator+(Vector lhs, const Vector& rhs) { lhs += rhs; return lhs; }, taking the left operand by value so it becomes a modifiable local copy that operator+= mutates and the function returns

exp: Taking the left-hand operand by value gives the function its own private copy, so lhs += rhs mutates only that copy, which is then returned; the caller's original a and b are untouched, exactly matching the value semantics expected of +. A is the classic bug hiding in plain sight: a member operator+ written as *this += rhs; return *this; silently mutates the left-hand operand of a + b, which no caller expects from +. B and C both try to call the non-const operator+= through a const Vector& parameter, which does not compile.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: A class declares `virtual ~Widget() = 0;` to force the class to be abstract, with no other pure virtual member. No definition of `~Widget` is supplied anywhere in the program. A derived class `Gadget` defines its own destructor, and the program creates and destroys a `Gadget` object. What happens?

opts.A: The program compiles and links; the base part of the object is destroyed without Widget::~Widget ever running.
opts.B: The program fails to compile, because a pure virtual function is not permitted to have a definition.
opts.C: The program compiles but fails to link, because destroying a Gadget still implicitly calls Widget::~Widget as part of the destruction chain, and a pure virtual destructor still needs a definition.
opts.D: The program compiles and links, but the base part of the object is destroyed twice.

exp: A derived class's destructor always implicitly calls its base class destructor after its own body runs, and that holds even for a pure virtual destructor — the '= 0' only forces Widget to be abstract, it does not excuse the compiler from needing a definition to call. Since Widget::~Widget() is declared but never defined, ~Gadget()'s implicit call to it leaves an unresolved symbol at link time. Option B is the trap: pure virtual functions are allowed to have definitions, and a pure virtual destructor in particular almost always needs one, since it is guaranteed to be invoked.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: Connection is an abstract class: it declares `virtual void send() = 0;` and no other pure virtual member. Which of the following definitions compiles?

opts.A: void transmit(const Connection& c) { }   (a function taking a reference)
opts.B: Connection make() { Connection c; return c; }   (returning one by value)
opts.C: void transmit(Connection c) { }   (a parameter taken by value)
opts.D: Connection buffer[4];   (an array of Connection)

exp: A reference parameter binds to an existing object without constructing a new one, so it is unaffected by Connection being abstract. Each other option makes the compiler create a complete, independent Connection — as a return value, as a by-value parameter, or as four default-constructed array elements — and an object of an abstract class cannot be created anywhere. Note the options are definitions on purpose: a bare declaration such as `Connection make();` compiles quite happily, because the restriction on abstract return and parameter types is enforced where the function is defined, not where it is declared.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: It compiles; Derived::step overrides Base::step in the usual way.
opts.B: It compiles; Derived::step hides Base::step rather than overriding it.
opts.C: It compiles only because Derived::step omits the `virtual` keyword; writing `virtual` back in would fail.
opts.D: It fails to compile, because Base::step is declared final and no further-derived class may declare a function matching that signature.

exp: final on a virtual function is a hard prohibition: any class deriving from Base that declares a function matching Base::step's signature is ill-formed, whether or not it repeats virtual or override. The failure is a compile error at the point Derived::step is declared, not a silent hide (B), and it has nothing to do with whether virtual is re-stated (C) — final blocks the override regardless.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
q: A class is declared `class D : protected B { ... };`. Which statement about the resulting access is correct?

opts.A: B's public members remain public in D, and only B's protected members become protected.
opts.B: B's public and protected members both become protected members of D — usable by D's own member functions and by classes further derived from D, but not by code outside the hierarchy.
opts.C: B's public and protected members become private members of D, and are inaccessible to any class derived from D.
opts.D: Protected inheritance affects only virtual function dispatch and leaves ordinary member access exactly as declared in B.

exp: Protected inheritance caps everything inherited at protected: both B's public and protected members become protected members of D, visible to D's own code and to D's further subclasses, but hidden from ordinary outside callers. Option A describes public inheritance, option C describes private inheritance, and option D is simply false — the inheritance kind changes access, not dispatch.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: Only d.show("hi") compiles; the other two remain hidden despite the using-declaration.
opts.B: None of the three compile, because a using-declaration cannot bring member functions into scope, only data members.
opts.C: All three compile, because `using Base::show;` pulls Base's show overloads into Derived's scope, where they overload alongside Derived::show(const char*) instead of being hidden by it.
opts.D: Only d.show(3) and d.show(3.5) compile; the using-declaration replaces Derived::show(const char*).

exp: Without the using-declaration, Derived::show(const char*) alone would hide every Base::show overload for lookup starting at Derived. The using-declaration explicitly re-introduces Base::show(int) and Base::show(double) into Derived's scope, so overload resolution sees all three signatures side by side and each call binds to the matching one. B is wrong because using-declarations routinely apply to member functions; D is wrong because the using-declaration adds overloads, it does not remove Derived's own.

sub: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects

opts.A: bp->notify(5);
opts.B: dp->notify(5);
opts.C: bp->notify();
opts.D: dp->notify();

exp: Member name lookup starts at the static type of the pointer used to make the call. Through dp, lookup starts at Derived's own scope, which only declares notify() with no parameters — Derived::notify() hides Base::notify(int) there, so dp->notify(5) has no matching overload and fails to compile. Through bp, lookup starts directly at Base's scope, where notify(int) is found untouched, so bp->notify(5) compiles fine: the hiding introduced inside Derived is invisible from a pointer whose static type is Base.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: A binary file store.dat holds fixed-size Record objects (assume sizeof(Record) exactly equals each record's on-disk size, with no padding) written back-to-back with no separators, and f is an already-open fstream on that file. Which call correctly positions the stream to read the 8th record (index 7, 0-based) directly, without reading any record before it?

opts.A: f.seekp(7 * sizeof(Record), ios::cur);
opts.B: f.seekg(7 * sizeof(Record), ios::beg);
opts.C: f.seekg(7, ios::beg);
opts.D: f.tellg(7 * sizeof(Record));

exp: seekg(offset, ios::beg) with offset = 7 * sizeof(Record) computes the absolute byte position of the 8th record and moves the get pointer that reading uses; the tempting option C treats the record index itself as a byte offset and lands inside record 0 instead of at the start of record 7. Option A moves the wrong pointer (seekp is for writing) by a relative amount, and D is not a valid call — tellg takes no argument, it only reports the current position.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: Employee is a struct of fixed-size members with no pointers and no virtual functions, and emp is an Employee variable. Which call correctly reads sizeof(emp) bytes from an already-open binary ifstream f directly into emp, and why does it need reinterpret_cast rather than static_cast?

opts.A: f.read(static_cast<char*>(&emp), sizeof(emp));
opts.B: f.read(&emp, sizeof(emp));
opts.C: f >> emp;
opts.D: f.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&emp), sizeof(emp));

exp: istream::read requires a char* destination, and Employee* is an unrelated pointer type with no implicit or static conversion path to char* — reinterpret_cast exists precisely to perform that low-level reinterpretation. Option A is the trap: static_cast only converts between related types (or through void*), so static_cast<char*>(&emp) is rejected by the compiler. Option B passes an Employee* where char* is required and fails to compile, and option C assumes an operator>> overload that a plain struct does not have.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP

opts.A: 25 2 — arr[0] and arr[1] are fully valid records; arr[2] has only its first 5 bytes overwritten from the file, and its remaining bytes are indeterminate.
opts.B: 30 3 — the read succeeds because arr provides enough room for all three records.
opts.C: 25 2 — but f.read() throws an exception because the file was shorter than requested, so this line never executes.
opts.D: 0 0 — reading past the requested size fails immediately and no bytes are transferred.

exp: f.gcount() reports the 25 bytes actually transferred before end-of-file, not the 30 requested, and 25 / sizeof(Rec) == 2 shows only arr[0] and arr[1] are complete; arr[2] ends up with its first 5 bytes overwritten and the rest indeterminate. Option C is the trap: istream::read never throws by default on a short read, it just sets eofbit and failbit, so execution reaches the cout line normally.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP

opts.A: [Alice] — getline always skips a single leading newline left behind by a previous >> extraction.
opts.B: compile error — std::getline cannot be called on a stream that a previous operator>> has already extracted from.
opts.C: [] — the newline left in the buffer after cin >> age extracts 30 is exactly the delimiter getline is looking for, so getline returns immediately with an empty string and "Alice" is never read this way.
opts.D: [30] — cin >> age consumes the entire first line including its newline, so getline goes on to read "Alice".

exp: cin >> age stops right after the digits and leaves the trailing '\n' sitting in the buffer; getline's default behaviour is to read up to and including its delimiter, and since that delimiter is the very next character, it returns an empty string without ever reaching "Alice". Option A is the trap — unlike >>, which skips leading whitespace before reading, getline does not skip a leading delimiter. The standard fix is an explicit cin.ignore(numeric_limits<streamsize>::max(), '\n') between the two calls.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: A hand-written parser calls int c = in.get(); to inspect the next character, then decides that character does not belong to the current token and must be the next one read again. Which single call correctly restores exactly that character to the stream?

opts.A: in.peek();
opts.B: in.putback(static_cast<char>(c));
opts.C: in.ignore();
opts.D: in.seekg(-1, ios::cur);

exp: putback(c) works purely at the level of the stream's internal buffer, pushing the character back so the next extraction reads it again, regardless of what device the stream is attached to. Option D is the trap: seekg repositions by asking the underlying stream buffer to reposition its data source, which fails and sets failbit on a non-seekable source such as cin attached to a terminal or pipe. peek() only inspects whatever character now follows in the stream and changes nothing, and ignore() discards a character going forward rather than restoring one.

sub: I/O streams and file handling in OOP
q: A line read from a file is const std::string line = "42,New Delhi,110001"; holding an id, a place name that itself contains a space, and a pincode. Using std::istringstream iss(line), which sequence correctly recovers id as int, place as std::string with its internal space intact, and pin as std::string?

opts.A: int id; std::string place, pin; iss >> id >> place >> pin;
opts.B: int id; std::string place, pin; std::getline(iss, place); iss >> id >> pin;
opts.C: int id; std::string place, pin; std::getline(iss, place, ','); iss >> id >> pin;
opts.D: int id; iss >> id; iss.ignore(1, ','); std::string place; std::getline(iss, place, ','); std::string pin; iss >> pin;

exp: Reading id first, discarding exactly the following comma with ignore(1, ','), then bounding the next getline at the following ',' is what keeps the embedded space in "New Delhi" intact while still stopping cleanly before "110001". Option A is the trap: plain iss >> place stops only at whitespace, so it swallows the leading comma into place as ",New" and leaves "Delhi,110001" for pin. Options B and C call getline before id is ever extracted, so they capture either the whole rest of the line or just "42" into place instead of the actual place name.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A try block contains a single handler, catch (...) { ... }. Which statement about that handler is correct?

opts.A: Inside the handler body there is no way to name or inspect the caught object, but a bare throw; still rethrows the exact exception that was caught
opts.B: It can only be used for exceptions of built-in type such as int or const char*, not for class-type exceptions
opts.C: It requires an exception-declaration naming std::exception, since (...) is shorthand for that type
opts.D: If the exception thrown is derived from std::exception, catch (...) does not match it; only a same-named catch (const std::exception&) does

exp: catch (...) matches any exception, including class types, but because the caught type is never named there is nothing to call what() or any other member function on inside the handler; it can still forward the untouched exception onward with a bare throw;. It is not restricted to built-in types and is not sugar for std::exception.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A constructor is written using a function-try-block: Widget::Widget(int n) try : buf_(n) { } catch (const std::bad_alloc&) { /* log it */ }. If the member-initialiser for buf_ throws std::bad_alloc, what happens once the catch block's body finishes executing?

opts.A: Construction succeeds anyway, because the catch block handled the exception, and the resulting Widget object is usable
opts.B: The exception is automatically rethrown to the constructor's caller once the handler finishes, because a function-try-block on a constructor cannot stop the exception from propagating
opts.C: The compiler treats reaching the end of the catch block as returning from the constructor normally, exactly as it would for an ordinary function's function-try-block
opts.D: A new object of type std::bad_alloc is thrown in place of the original exception, discarding the original

exp: For a constructor's (or destructor's) function-try-block, reaching the end of the handler always rethrows the exception that was caught — the language never lets a constructor 'succeed' after one of its subobjects failed to initialise. This is exactly where function-try-block semantics differ from an ordinary function, where falling off the end of the handler would just return normally.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: Which statement about the <stdexcept>/<new> exception hierarchy is correct?

opts.A: std::out_of_range derives from std::runtime_error, and std::bad_alloc derives from std::runtime_error as well
opts.B: std::bad_alloc derives from std::logic_error, since insufficient memory can be predicted in advance by checking available resources
opts.C: std::out_of_range derives from std::logic_error, and std::bad_alloc derives directly from std::exception rather than from std::runtime_error
opts.D: std::out_of_range and std::bad_alloc both derive directly from std::exception, bypassing logic_error and runtime_error entirely

exp: std::out_of_range is one of the logic_error subclasses in <stdexcept>, while std::bad_alloc is declared in <new> as a direct subclass of std::exception — it sits under neither logic_error nor runtime_error, since an allocation failure is not a predictable caller bug.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: A function offers the basic exception guarantee but not the strong guarantee. If the function throws partway through, what is guaranteed?

opts.A: The operation either completes fully or has no observable effect at all, as if it had never been called
opts.B: The function is guaranteed not to throw at all under any circumstances
opts.C: Only the memory allocated during the call is guaranteed to be freed; other data members may be left in an invalid, undefined state
opts.D: No resources are leaked and every object involved remains in some valid, destructible state, but the values it held before the call are not guaranteed to be restored

exp: The basic guarantee promises only that nothing leaks and every object stays in some valid, usable state after a partial failure — it does not promise the pre-call values are restored. That commit-or-rollback promise is the strong guarantee (option A), and never throwing at all describes the no-throw guarantee (option B), a stronger property still.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: Given std::string s = "hi"; auto it = s.begin(); char& r = s[0]; s.push_back('!'); — assume this push_back triggers a reallocation of the string's buffer. What is the status of it and r afterward?

opts.A: Both it and r are invalidated; using either afterward is undefined behaviour
opts.B: it is invalidated but r remains valid, because operator[] returns a reference bound directly to a character rather than to the string's buffer
opts.C: Both remain valid, because std::string guarantees contiguous storage is never moved by push_back
opts.D: r is invalidated but it remains valid, since iterators are position-based offsets recomputed automatically after reallocation

exp: A reallocating push_back invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the old buffer — operator[]'s reference and begin()'s iterator are both just views into that same storage, so both die together. Contiguous storage is not the same guarantee as storage never moving, and iterators are not magically recomputed after a move.

sub: Exception handling and strings
q: For a std::string s of length 5, consider s.substr(3, 10) and s.substr(10, 1). What happens in each case?

opts.A: Both calls throw std::out_of_range, because the requested length in each case exceeds the number of characters actually available
opts.B: s.substr(3, 10) returns the 2 remaining characters from position 3 to the end, with the count silently clamped; s.substr(10, 1) throws std::out_of_range because 10 exceeds s.size()
opts.C: Both calls silently clamp to whatever characters are available, and neither ever throws, since substr never validates its position argument
opts.D: s.substr(3, 10) throws because the count exceeds the string, while s.substr(10, 1) silently returns an empty string

exp: substr(pos, count) throws std::out_of_range only when pos exceeds size(); the count argument is simply clamped to whichever characters remain and never itself causes a throw. pos=3 is within a 5-character string, so it returns the 2 available characters, while pos=10 fails that bounds check and throws.
